content.body: Ever tried to piece together a travel itinerary from a pile of tickets? That's exactly what we'll do today. We'll learn how to reconstruct a complete journey from scattered flight segments using a clever memory technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply a hash map to track departure and arrival points.
• Implement an algorithm to find the correct travel order.
• Explain why we check the map before adding new information.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: You have tickets: [['MUC','LHR'], ['JFK','MUC']]. What's the full itinerary starting from JFK?
content.successMessage: Great! JFK → MUC → LHR is correct.

content.title: Try a bigger set
content.prompt: Tickets: [['ATL','EWR'], ['SFO','ATL'], ['JFK','SFO']]. Start from JFK. What's the full route?
content.successMessage: Well done! JFK → SFO → ATL → EWR works.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: Tickets: [['LAX','SFO'], ['JFK','LAX'], ['SFO','JFK']]. Start from JFK. Can you trace it?
content.successMessage: Excellent! You manually connected JFK → LAX → SFO → JFK.

content.body: You just manually traced paths by looking at each ticket and finding connections. That's like sorting physical tickets on a table—it works for a few, but gets messy with hundreds.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With thousands of tickets, manually matching departures to arrivals becomes impossible. We need a systematic way to remember connections without re-scanning everything. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. We'll use a lookup structure (a Map) to note departure points and their destinations. This acts like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll build the itinerary by tracking start and end points in a hash map, then follow the chain from the starting airport.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Example: [['MUC','LHR'], ['JFK','MUC']].
1. Build map: MUC→LHR, JFK→MUC.
2. Find start: JFK (not a destination in map).
3. Follow chain: JFK→MUC→LHR.
Key: We store departure as key, arrival as value. Check map to find next destination quickly.

content.body:
1. Create a Map to store tickets (departure → arrival).
2. Identify the starting airport (it's a departure not used as a destination elsewhere).
3. Follow the chain: from start, use map to get next airport, repeat until done.
4. Collect airports in order to build the itinerary.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called findItinerary that takes tickets array and returns the itinerary as an array of airports.
steps.hint: Start with function definition and return an empty array for now.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function skeleton.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure the function is named findItinerary and takes tickets parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need function findItinerary(tickets) that returns an array.

steps.title: Create the lookup map
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create a Map called flights. Loop through tickets and store each departure as key and arrival as value.
steps.hint: Use new Map() and a for...of loop to populate it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! The map now remembers each departure's destination.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your loop syntax. Use for (const [from, to] of tickets).
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: flights.set(from, to) adds each ticket to the map.

steps.title: Find the starting airport
steps.instruction: The starting airport is a departure that isn't a destination in any ticket. Find it by checking all map keys against all values.
steps.hint: Create a Set of all destinations, then find a key not in that set.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've identified the unique starting point.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure to check each key against the destinations set.
steps.feedbackWrong: The start is a key in flights that doesn't appear in destinations.

steps.title: Follow the chain
steps.instruction: Now build the itinerary array. Start from the start airport, then repeatedly get the next airport from the flights map until there's no more.
steps.hint: Use a while loop that continues while flights.has(current).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You're following the chain using the map lookup.
steps.feedbackPartial: Don't forget to push the current airport in each loop iteration.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loop should continue while the map has the current airport as a key.

steps.title: Return the result
steps.instruction: Finally, return the itinerary array from your function.
steps.hint: Simply return itinerary instead of the empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully implemented the itinerary reconstruction.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure you're returning the itinerary array, not an empty one.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function should return the itinerary variable.

content.body: Congratulations! You've learned how to reconstruct an itinerary using a hash map to remember connections. Key takeaways: we store departures as keys and arrivals as values, check the map to find next destinations, and follow the chain from the unique starting point. This 'notebook' approach avoids re-scanning all tickets repeatedly.
content.title: Done
